To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we developed a permutation test to evaluate whether a species is affected by interspecific competition, and 2) we found that the identity matters at the phylogenetic family level rather than at the species level.

(1) the identity of a focal tree’s neighbors matters to its growth rate, (2) the identity of those neighbors is more important at the family level than at the species level, and (3) the identity of focal and neighbor trees is important to growth at all sizes of trees.

(1) we found a significant effect of species identity on the competitive effect, but (2) the identity effect is strongest at the family level rather than the species level, and (3) the spatial cross-validation scheme is computationally feasible for our model and can be used in other models of interspecific interactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to best estimate and evaluate models of interspecific interactions.
the development of a new approach for measuring species-specific competitive interactions and the application of this approach to a forest dynamics plot.
the estimation of species interactions and the spatial cross-validation of these models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
species-specific competitive effects do not exist, and that instead, species-specific competitive effects are a function of phylogenetic distance.
species-level competition matters, but the identity of species matters less than the identity of families.
species identity does not matter for competitive interactions in this forest, but that phylogenetic relatedness of species does.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
species-specific competitive effects can be estimated with repeat censused large permanent plots.
species-specific interactions are not the best level at which to model competition, but that the identity of a competitor does matter.
the identity of a competitor matters for the growth of a focal tree, but the identity of the competitor is less important than its size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spatial cross-validation can be an effective tool for assessing models of interspecific competitive interactions, even in cases where the number of interactions is very large.
we can use repeat-censused plots to test for the presence of species-specific competitive interactions and to quantify them, even in large plots with many species.
we provide a new approach to measuring interspecific competition, which is a critical component of understanding the structure and dynamics of plant communities.
